title: Pre-Purchase Ship Inspection Piraeus | Perama & Anchorage
description: Pre-purchase inspection in Piraeus for buyers of bulk carriers, tankers and ferries sold by Greek owners: anchorage, Perama quays and Elefsina bay.
h1: Inspecting a Second-Hand Ship Before Subjects Are Lifted: Piraeus, Perama and Elefsina
intro: Piraeus sits at the centre of the second-hand market. Greek owners are among the busiest buyers and sellers of bulk carriers and tankers, so ships for sale lie at the outer anchorage, in Elefsina bay or alongside the Perama repair quays while buyers decide. A pre-purchase inspection here has to be quick, measured and readable by people who know the ship type well: spot thickness readings, crack checks, coatings, hatch covers and machinery condition, gathered before subjects are lifted. The Atlantis team travels from India on Schengen visas, so early notice of the viewing date matters.

highlights.h: Ships viewed where Greek sellers keep them
highlights.p: A ship coming out of a Greek fleet is usually shown where her managers can attend: the Piraeus anchorage, a waiting or lay-up position in Elefsina bay, or the Perama quays during afloat repairs. Each place allows a different depth of inspection, and the plan follows from it.

highlights.h: Ages that bring heavy survey scopes
highlights.p: Many bulk carriers and tankers sold out of Greek fleets are around 15 to 20 years old, with a third or fourth renewal survey ahead. Measured readings in the areas those surveys gauge most heavily show the buyer what the new owner is likely to face.

Ro-pax ferries change hands between operators, and the best time to see one is the winter lay-up at Piraeus or Perama, when vehicle decks are empty, voids can be opened and machinery is under maintenance rather than racing to the next island.

sections.h: Where can a buyer view a ship around Piraeus?
p: The outer anchorage off Piraeus is the usual meeting point for a buyer's inspection on a bulk carrier or tanker that is between voyages or waiting for the sale to complete. The team goes out by launch arranged by the seller's agent and works on what the crew has prepared: holds cleaned and ventilated, ballast tanks certified for entry, deck and hatch covers open to view.

Elefsina bay, a short way north-west, has long held ships that are idle, laid up or waiting for a buyer. A ship lying there with a reduced crew can be slower to prepare: ventilation fans may be stopped, lighting in tanks has to be rigged and the generators may be started only for the readings. Those limits are agreed with the seller's technical department before the visit, so the buyer knows in advance which spaces will be seen.

The Perama repair zone gives the most access, because sellers often carry out repairs before delivery. A ship afloat at the quays may already have tanks open and staging up, and a ship in a PPA floating dock shows bottom plating, sea chests and the rudder area while she is dry. Repairs under way can hide as much as they reveal, though, so fresh paint and new steel are noted as such in the report.

Elefsina bay: idle and laid-up ships, with access set by the crew and the power available on board
Perama quays: ships under afloat repair, where open tanks and staging widen what can be checked

sections.h: Which ships change hands through Piraeus, and what do buyers need to know?
p: Greek owners buy second-hand tonnage, trade it hard and sell it on, so the ships inspected here for a buyer are often Handysize, Supramax, Panamax and Kamsarmax bulk carriers in the second half of their working lives, and crude, product and chemical tankers approaching the age limits that oil majors and charterers apply. The buyer may be another Greek owner, a buyer from Asia, the Middle East or elsewhere in Europe, or a lender backing either.

For a ship of that age the important questions concern the next renewal survey and the next charterer. How much steel will the holds, hopper tanks and topside tanks need at the third or fourth special survey? Are the ballast tank coatings still FAIR, or already POOR and heading for renewal? Will a tanker find charterers without a CAP rating, and if not, what will the CAP survey find? A walk-round cannot answer these; readings in the right places can at least narrow the range.

Ferries are a separate market. Ro-pax ships move between Greek island operators and to buyers abroad, and they are bought on the condition of their vehicle decks, ramps, doors, voids and machinery as much as the hull. The inspection there is planned around the lay-up, when the ship is quiet.

sections.h: Working with the seller's technical department before subjects are lifted
p: In Piraeus the seller's superintendent is often on board for the buyer's visit, and the arrangements are made directly with the seller's technical department through the brokers. That helps: they know the ship, they can authorise tank entry and the running of machinery, and they can produce the planned maintenance records and the last thickness reports on the spot.

It also makes the boundaries clear from the start. Opening up, grinding a patch for crack detection or lifting a hatch panel for a closer look are each requested through the buyer, and refusals are recorded rather than argued. Because the seller's people work in the same city, a question raised on board in the morning can often be answered from their files by the afternoon, which keeps the short decision period after inspection useful.

sections.h: What does a Piraeus pre-purchase inspection tell a buyer about the next special survey?
p: On a bulk carrier heading for her third or fourth renewal survey, the team concentrates readings where class will gauge most heavily: lower hold frames and brackets, hopper and topside tank plating, the lower strakes of transverse bulkheads, hatch coaming tops and deck plating between hatches. Grab damage, distorted frames and wastage under scale are photographed, and hatch corners and bracket toes are checked for cracks wherever the seller allows a patch to be cleaned.

On a tanker, cargo tanks are usually not gas-free, so the double-bottom and wing ballast tanks carry the inspection, with readings on the inner bottom, side shell and the upper parts of the tanks under the deck. Comparing these with the last renewal survey readings, which the seller can release through class, shows how fast the steel is going. For a buyer weighing the next five years, that rate matters more than any single reading.

Many Greek-managed bulk carriers and tankers had scrubbers fitted early, and those installations now have several years of service behind them. Their wash-water and overboard lines are worth gauging during the visit, especially near bends and the shell connection, because they are among the first repairs a new owner meets.

sections.h: Inspecting a ro-pax ferry for a buyer during winter lay-up in Piraeus
p: A ferry buyer wants to know how the ship has stood up to years of short crossings, heavy vehicle traffic and summer peaks. With the ship laid up, the vehicle decks can be walked empty and their plating gauged where trailers and lashings concentrate wear, and ramp and door hinges can be examined, with magnetic particle checks on accessible lugs if the seller agrees. Void spaces and ballast tanks under the vehicle decks, where condensation and leaks collect, are opened in sequence with the crew.

Machinery on a laid-up ferry may be partly dismantled for winter maintenance, so readings are taken on whatever the chief engineer can run, and the maintenance records show what has been opened and what was found. Opening up for the buyer still needs the seller's consent, but anything the repairers have already opened can be seen and photographed, which often gives a ferry buyer more than a trading ship ever would.

sections.h: Planning the visit: Schengen visas, launches and the viewing date
p: The team travels from India on Schengen visas, so the earlier the viewing window is known, the safer the plan. Brokers often know some days or weeks ahead that a ship will be at the anchorage or in Perama; sending us the vessel name and the expected dates at that stage lets the visa application run while the terms are still being discussed.

Launches, gate passes for the PPA areas and ISPS clearance are arranged by the seller's agent. Send the class records and the seller's last thickness report if the brokers already hold them: reading them before boarding means the time on board goes on measuring rather than searching, and the team arrives knowing which areas the last survey flagged.

faqs.q: Can you inspect a ship laid up in Elefsina bay for a buyer?
faqs.a: Yes, with the seller's agreement and enough power on board. A laid-up ship often runs with a small crew, so ventilation, lighting and the generators needed for machinery readings have to be arranged in advance. We agree with the seller's technical department which spaces will be ready, and the report lists anything that could not be entered safely and why.

faqs.q: Will the seller's superintendent be present during the inspection in Piraeus?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Greek sellers commonly send their own superintendent to accompany a buyer's inspection, which makes it easier to obtain entry permits, run machinery and see the maintenance records. The team still works only for the buyer: findings go to the buyer and the buyer's broker, and what the seller's people say on board is recorded as information, not as evidence.

faqs.q: Can you check a ship being repaired at Perama before delivery?
faqs.a: Yes, and the repair period often allows more access than a trading call: tanks may be open, staging in place and, in a floating dock, the bottom visible. Repairs under way need care. New steel, fresh coatings and unfinished work are recorded separately, so the buyer can see what was original condition and what the seller's yard work has changed.

faqs.q: Does the inspection help with a tanker that will need a CAP rating?
faqs.a: It gives the buyer an early indication. Readings in the ballast tanks and on deck, compared with the last renewal survey thickness report, show where the steel is heading, and that is what a CAP survey examines in detail. It cannot predict the rating, which class issues after its own survey. Pre-purchase readings serve the buyer's decision and are not credited to class; Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS.

faqs.q: Can a ro-pax ferry be inspected for a buyer during the summer season?
faqs.a: It can, but expect far less. In season a ferry turns round in hours with vehicles and passengers on board, so the visit is limited to the engine room, open decks and records. Winter lay-up at Piraeus or Perama is the better time, when vehicle decks, voids and tanks are accessible and the chief engineer has time to run machinery for readings.

faqs.q: How early should a buyer contact you for a ship at Piraeus?
faqs.a: As soon as the brokers have a vessel name and a likely viewing window. The team needs Schengen visas issued in India, and the visa appointment is usually the longest step. Send the IMO number, where she will lie, the dates and the buyer's priorities to info@atlantisndt.com or through the form on this page, and we plan travel against the ship's programme.
